title: Theo and the Choir
premise: Tamsin Sandoval, a runaway hedge-witch's apprentice hiding his magic in the anti-magical city of Vell, finds a mute child on his doorstep who speaks only in the First Tongue—the language that once commanded reality itself. As the moon's thirteenth turn approaches, Tamsin discovers the boy is a living vessel of the Choir, a collective memory that the old kingdoms burned out to end their war, and that Vell's ruling Conclave wants him silenced forever. Hunted by an inquisitor who was once his closest friend, Tamsin must choose between surrendering the child and teaching him to sing—knowing the song will erase one memory from every listener to pay for its power. In the end, Tamsin offers his own twelve years of hiding as the price: the city forgets its hatred of magic, the boy is freed as an ordinary child, and Tamsin walks out of Vell remembering nothing of why he ever ran.
about_author: Orsen Oyelaran is a former church archivist from Lagos who spent a decade cataloguing hymnals in three dead languages before turning to fiction. He writes fantasy about what communities choose to remember, and lives quietly with a parrot that refuses to learn any word older than itself.

chapters.title: The Boy at the Door
chapters.summary: POV Tamsin. On a rain-lashed night, a mute child appears at Tamsin's charm-shop door speaking words that make his wards flare for the first time in twelve years. The beat is dread wrapped in tenderness: Tamsin recognizes the First Tongue from his apprenticeship and knows exactly how much danger just walked in.

chapters.title: Charms for a Lawful City
chapters.summary: POV Tamsin. Flashback-tinged chapter establishing Vell's Edict of Silence and Tamsin's careful double life selling 'luck' that is really nothing at all. When a Conclave inspector browses his shop, the emotional beat is the exhaustion of permanent concealment—and the first crack in it.

chapters.title: What the Moon Counts
chapters.summary: POV Tamsin. An old almanac reveals the moon enters its thirteenth turn in under a year, the interval in which, legend says, the Choir can be rekindled or killed. Tamsin tries to convince himself the boy is coincidence. The beat is denial curdling into responsibility.

chapters.title: Inquisitor Ilsa Vane
chapters.summary: POV Ilsa. The Conclave's chief inquisitor senses a resonance in the low quarter and begins her sweep. Through her eyes we see she genuinely believes magic murdered her family. The beat is sympathy for the antagonist: she is right about the danger and wrong about everything else.

chapters.title: Lessons in a Dead Language
chapters.summary: POV Tamsin. Tamsin teaches the boy—whom he names Theo—basic words, and each spoken syllable bends small realities: bread rises unasked, a broken cup knits. Wonder and terror share the page; Tamsin realizes he isn't hiding a child, he's raising a weapon someone built.

chapters.title: The Hedge-Witch's Last Letter
chapters.summary: POV Tamsin. A letter from Tamsin's old mistress, posthumously delivered, warns that the Choir was never destroyed—only scattered into children—and begs him to let it sleep. The beat is betrayal across the grave: the woman who taught him also helped bury this.

chapters.title: Ashes on the Register
chapters.summary: POV Ilsa. Ilsa finds records of eleven other 'resonant' children born across two decades—all dead of ordinary causes, all too convenient. Her certainty wavers for the first time. The beat is the first hairline fracture in her faith in the Conclave.

chapters.title: A Market of Small Magics
chapters.summary: POV Tamsin. Desperate for allies, Tamsin visits the underground market of hidden practitioners and is refused help—everyone remembers the last war's cost. Only a disgraced choir-singer, Maren, agrees to listen to Theo. The beat is loneliness answered at a terrible price.

chapters.title: Maren's Voice
chapters.summary: POV Maren. The exiled singer hears Theo hum a fragment and weeps, recognizing the descant her order died preserving. She explains the Choir's bargain: its songs rewrite memory to fuel miracles. The beat is awe shadowed by grief—she lost her voice to the Edict and may lose more now.

chapters.title: The Thirteenth Turn Begins
chapters.summary: POV Tamsin. The moon marks its turn; Theo's speech bursts open overnight and objects near him begin remembering former shapes—a chair becoming a sapling, walls sweating mortar. The beat is acceleration: the countdown everyone feared has audibly started.

chapters.title: Ilsa Closes the Net
chapters.summary: POV Ilsa. A raid on the underground market yields Maren's name; Ilsa interrogates her old friend and finds mercy she cannot afford. The beat is duty versus doubt—Ilsa files the report that will doom the quarter while hating herself for the accuracy of it.

chapters.title: Flight Across the Rooftops
chapters.summary: POV Tamsin. Conclave soldiers reach the shop; Tamsin flees with Theo through burning tenements, using forbidden magic openly for the first time in twelve years. The beat is liberation and loss entwined—he saves the boy by destroying the life he built to be safe.

chapters.title: The Conclave's True Archive
chapters.summary: POV Ilsa. Deep in the Conclave vaults, Ilsa discovers the Edict wasn't peace—it was amnesia imposed on an entire civilization, and the war ended because no one could remember why they fought. The beat is vertigo: her whole moral architecture was built on a deletion.

chapters.title: Refuge at the Salt Chapel
chapters.summary: POV Tamsin. Hiding in a ruined chapel, Tamsin and Theo grow close; Theo, learning words, asks why people fear him. Tamsin lies badly. The beat is intimacy poisoned by secrecy—the reader sees the ending's price being quietly set.

chapters.title: Maren's Bargain
chapters.summary: POV Maren. Rescued before execution, Maren proposes completing the Choir deliberately but controlled: thirteen singers, one memory surrendered per verse. She names Tamsin as first singer. The beat is horror dressed as hope—the cure requires the disease.

chapters.title: The Conclave Marches
chapters.summary: POV Ilsa. Ordered to lead the purge personally, Ilsa instead steals the archive's memory-engine core and defects, arriving at the chapel as neither ally nor enemy. The beat is conversion without absolution—she changes sides knowing she can never be forgiven.

chapters.title: Thirteen Voices
chapters.summary: POV Tamsin. Hidden practitioners, defectors, and even repentant Conclave clerks gather; the rehearsal begins and the chapel fills with impossible harmonies. The beat is communal joy—the book's warmest chapter, placed deliberately before the fall.

chapters.title: The Verse That Takes
chapters.summary: POV Maren. The first full verse works: a dying singer is healed, and half the congregation forgets their own weddings. Maren understands the Choir cannot be aimed, only spent. The beat is grief-stricken clarity—the plan is monstrous at any scale.

chapters.title: Siege of the Salt Chapel
chapters.summary: POV Ilsa. The Conclave army arrives; Ilsa turns the memory-engine against her former order, buying hours at the cost of her own past. The beat is sacrifice as identity-erasure made literal—she fights for people she can no longer remember loving.

chapters.title: Theo Chooses
chapters.summary: POV Theo (rendered in his new language). Theo, now fluent, grasps what the final verse demands and offers himself as the entire payment—but Tamsin steps into the circle first, singing the counter-melody his mistress taught him. The beat is the climax: love outbidding sacrifice.

chapters.title: The Song of Forgetting
chapters.summary: POV Tamsin. The completed Choir rises over Vell; the city's hatred of magic dissolves as Tamsin's twelve hidden years are consumed as payment. He watches himself become a stranger mid-song. The beat is transcendent loss—the theme of memory paid in full.

chapters.title: A Shop With No Keeper
chapters.summary: POV Ilsa, coda. Months later, a peaceful Vell; Ilsa, keeper of the restored archive, finds an ordinary boy named Theo leaving flowers at a shuttered charm-shop, and a man with no past walking out the city gate toward somewhere green. The beat is bittersweet resolution: the world healed, the healer forgotten.
